I have to calculate the sample size for an experimental study and took some sample distributions data from a previous similar research and calculated the means and standard variations for before and after the treatment (see picture). since the sample distribution is not normally distributed, does it still make sense to calculate the standard deviation? is it common to use the effect size from previous studies or should one even lower the effect size for sample size calculation? how do I process further in order to get a sample size, whit power of 80%, alpha .05? The outcomes represent the payouts that come with the reports done by the participants. But how does one come up with the answer? I was actually going try to compare the means, but since the outcome distributions are not normally distributed I guess one has to use non parametric test. **Understanding current data.** It looks as if the counts from your previous experiment may have. is for the control group and the second for the treatment group,. and columns are for 0 through 5. that scores 0-5 are independent of group, with P-value 0.002. But this does not say that scores are higher in the treatment group, only that the distributions differ--as one can readily. The lists of individual scores for treatment and control. `x.t = rep(0:5, times=n.t). x.c = rep(0:5, times=n.c). data: x.t and x.c. W = 3068.5, p-value = 0.001552. However, empirical CDF plots show that the treatment scores (blue) 'stochastically dominate' the control scores; that is, the treatment ECDF is (mainly) to the right of the control ECDF (thus below it on the cumulative probability graph). **Power and sample size.** From the one prior experiment of this kind we can guess. more efficient to have equal sample sizes in the treatment and control groups, so I will start with $n\_t = n\_c = 75.$.
